components.primer: Air power and integrated air and missile defense depend on sensing, command and control, weapons, basing, sustainment, and cross-domain support. Cost exchange, magazine depth, and aircraft availability are central modern research questions.

Airlift is fast but capacity-limited relative to sealift. Aerial ports and en route infrastructure are binding constraints. In high-threat environments, airlift may preserve options for critical cargo while remaining unable to replace bulk sealift.

AI and uncrewed systems change sensing, scale, cost exchange, tempo, and human-machine teaming. Claims require careful scoping because capabilities and countermeasures adapt rapidly. Separate acquisition oversight evidence from battlefield observation and strategic AI risk literature. **Drone technical & administrative sub-corpus:** This component also holds FAA Part 107 administration (remote pilot certification, airspace, weather, maintenance, waivers), state UAS security requirements, educational platform technical manuals, GAO NAS-integration and remote-ID oversight, and open RAND analyses of UAS training, sUAS capabilities, and swarms. Treat certification materials as regulatory/training evidence, not combat TTPs.

Command and control literature examines authority, intent, decision rights, information flow, degraded communications, and adaptation. Modern systems should be studied as socio-technical organizations rather than software alone. Centralization vs. mission command is a recurring trade under EW and high tempo.

Open literature discusses A2/AD pressure on access, basing, and logistics without providing targeting data. Analysis should use aggregate risk measures, campaign vignettes, and public wargame insights rather than operational vulnerability details of live systems.

Cyberspace and electromagnetic-spectrum operations interact with communications, sensing, navigation, and command. This library keeps analysis defensive and conceptual, excluding weaponized code and live-system vulnerabilities. Public lessons emphasize jamming, PNT denial, and software-dependent weapons.

Logistics IT outages reduce planning quality even when physical assets remain. Manual fallbacks are slow. Modern warfare research links enterprise software modernization, weapon-system cyber, and supply-chain risk.

Joint logistics integrates service capabilities to project and sustain forces. Public doctrine emphasizes visibility, throughput, and prioritization under uncertainty. Apply to modern warfare by testing how doctrine assumptions hold when ports, cyber systems, and industrial surge are simultaneously stressed.

Bulk fuel underwrites operational tempo. Pipeline, tanker, and storage shocks cascade into ops design. Contested logistics analysis should treat fuel as a multi-node system with financial, physical, and cyber failure modes.

Industrial surge is a multi-month or multi-year remedy. Protracted conflict literature from Ukraine and Russia shows production adaptation, supplier dependencies, and workforce limits dominate long-war outcomes.

Information affects understanding, behavior, legitimacy, cohesion, and decision advantage. Research must distinguish verifiable effects from assumed influence and avoid operational manipulation guidance. Digital C2 and public narratives both matter in contemporary wars.

Inland LOCs (truck/rail) convert port discharge into combat power. Bridges, security, chassis balance, and border processes matter. Persistent surveillance and long-range fires raise the cost of dense, predictable logistics traffic.

ISR turns collection into decision-relevant understanding through prioritization, processing, exploitation, analysis, dissemination, and feedback. More sensing can increase overload unless linked to decisions. Transparent battlefields raise both opportunity and deception risk.

Joint and multidomain doctrine explains how effects across land, maritime, air, space, cyberspace, and the information environment are integrated. Doctrine is authoritative guidance, not evidence that execution will match the ideal. Test claims against recent-conflict observations and C2 constraints.

Land and urban operations combine maneuver, fires, engineering, protection, sustainment, information, and civilian considerations. Urban terrain compresses military and civilian systems and amplifies second-order effects under persistent ISR and drones.

Modern-warfare analysis must include international humanitarian law, civilian harm mitigation, and cascading effects of damage to essential services. Legal and humanitarian sources provide necessary constraints and outcome measures for any campaign literature review.

Lessons from ongoing and recent conflicts are observations, not universal laws. Preserve publication date, evidence quality, theater conditions, adversary capabilities, and the difference between adaptation and durable change. Prefer multi-source triangulation across RAND, CSIS, RUSI, and official oversight.

Maritime and littoral warfare combines sea control, denial, strike, protection, logistics, and commercial traffic constraints. Recent Red Sea and blockade wargames should not be generalized without accounting for geography and force composition.

Ammunition distribution is a timed pipeline from industrial production through depots and ASPs. Modern high-intensity war shows magazine depth, production lead times, and safety/security rules as campaign-limiting factors.

Ports are multi-actor systems (military, commercial, labor, host nation). Throughput is brittle to labor, cyber, and physical shocks. Seabasing and alternate discharge methods appear in public literature as partial mitigations, not complete substitutes.

Prepositioned stocks trade early availability against access, maintenance, and political permission to issue. Modern warfare literature asks whether prepo remains survivable and usable under long-range strike, cyber interference, and host-nation friction.

Strategic sealift moves the bulk of heavy unit equipment and sustainment. Contested sea lines of communication impose escort demands and chokepoint delays. For modern peer conflict, treat sealift readiness, commercial capacity, and port access as campaign variables rather than background assumptions.

Spacepower enables positioning, timing, communications, missile warning, and intelligence while also operating as a contested domain. The library focuses on doctrine, resilience, commercial SSA, and Ukraine-derived public observations rather than sensitive architectures.

Strategy sources connect political objectives, deterrence, force posture, alliances, escalation risk, and resource choices. Treat strategy documents as policy positions tied to publication dates; compare with independent analysis of industrial capacity and theater geography.
